passage:
Monday: Arnab, sixteen, forwarded a message to his class group: "Drinking cold water after meals causes serious illness." Yamini replied, "Source?" Arnab typed, "Everyone knows this," and felt annoyed that she was questioning him in front of everyone.
Wednesday: Still irritated, he searched to prove her wrong. Every reliable site he found said the claim had no evidence. He noticed he had been hunting only for pages that agreed with him.
The next Monday: He posted, "I was wrong about the cold water thing. I believed it because my Nani says it, and I didn't check." Yamini sent a thumbs up. Arnab felt strangely lighter.

qa.q: What did Yamini reply to Arnab's message?
qa.a: She replied, "Source?"

qa.q: Why did Arnab feel annoyed on Monday?
qa.a: He felt challenged in front of everyone, and his confidence in the message made the question feel like an attack.

qa.q: What was the key moment of change for Arnab?
qa.a: Noticing he had been searching only for pages that agreed with him, which let him see his own bias.

qa.q: How might Yamini see Arnab's public correction?
qa.a: She probably respects him more for admitting he was wrong, which is why she sent a thumbs up.

grounding: It shows a teenager noticing his own confirmation bias and publicly admitting the limits of what he knew.

passage: Arnab, when I was fifteen, I was sure my best friend Neelam hated me. She didn't wave one morning, and by lunch I had decided she was jealous of my marks. I felt it so strongly that it had to be true. I stopped talking to her for two weeks. Then her brother said, "Jyoti, our grandmother was in hospital that week." She hadn't even seen me that morning. I remember sitting on the school steps, hot-faced, realising that a strong feeling had made me certain, not any fact. Since then, when I'm very sure about what someone thinks, I ask myself: what do I actually know? Usually it's much less than I feel.

qa.q: How long did young Jyoti stop talking to Neelam?
qa.a: For two weeks.

qa.q: What did Jyoti realise, hot-faced, on the school steps?
qa.a: That a strong feeling, not any fact, had made Jyoti certain about Neelam's motives, and it brought shame.

qa.q: What question does Jyoti now ask herself, and why does it help?
qa.a: "What do I actually know?" It separates facts from feelings before deciding what someone thinks.

qa.q: How might Neelam have experienced those two weeks?
qa.a: Already worried about her grandmother, she probably felt confused and hurt that her friend suddenly went cold.

grounding: It shows, told by an elder, a teenager recognising that emotional reasoning had created certainty without facts.

passage: The physics project was due at nine the next morning, and the lab readings made no sense. Bidisha, seventeen, was sure her method was right; she'd topped the last test. When Suraj said, "Maybe we measured the length wrong," she snapped, "I did that part. It's fine." It was eleven at night and the power kept flickering. Suraj quietly re-measured by torchlight. Four centimetres off. Bidisha stared at the ruler. Her face burned. She thought of how quickly she'd dismissed him, just because she'd done well before. "You're right. I was sure because I'm usually right, which isn't a reason." They redid the graph by one in the morning. It came out straight.

qa.q: How far off was the measurement?
qa.a: Four centimetres.

qa.q: What did Bidisha realise about herself when she stared at the ruler?
qa.a: That her certainty came from past success rather than checking, and she felt embarrassed for dismissing Suraj.

qa.q: What could Bidisha do in future group work?
qa.a: Treat a teammate's doubt as a reason to check rather than a challenge, especially under time pressure.

qa.q: How might Suraj have felt when she snapped at him?
qa.a: Brushed off, yet he chose to re-measure quietly rather than argue, which kept the project on track.

grounding: It shows a teenager recognising overconfidence as a bias and admitting the limits of her knowledge under deadline pressure.

passage: Varun had been sure since Monday: the new chemistry teacher disliked him. She had cut four marks on his practical file, and he told everyone at the Salt Lake bus stop. On Thursday, Deepika showed him her file. Four marks cut too, for the same missing diagrams. 'She wrote the same comment on mine,' Deepika said. Varun felt his face heat up. He opened his file again and actually read the red ink. It was specific, even polite. 'I think I decided she hated me because I felt bad,' he said slowly, 'and then I only noticed things that fit.' Deepika grinned. 'So, apologise to the bus stop?' 'Maybe just redraw the diagrams first.'

qa.q: How many marks were cut from Varun's file?
qa.a: Four marks were cut.

qa.q: What made Varun's face heat up?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed once Deepika's file showed the same cut and comment, proving his story about the teacher was wrong.

qa.q: What habit could help Varun next time he feels treated unfairly?
qa.a: He could read the actual feedback and compare with others before deciding someone is against him.

qa.q: What would change if Varun had kept telling his story at the bus stop?
qa.a: Other students might have started seeing the teacher as unfair without reason, hurting her start at the school.

grounding: Shows a teenager recognising that his hurt feelings shaped his belief and that he only noticed evidence that fit it.

passage:
'Auto is always faster than the bus to Nani's. Always.'
'Payal, last week the auto took forty minutes,' said her brother Amandeep, not looking up from his laptop.
'That was one time. Traffic.'
'And the one time you took the bus?'
'...It came quickly. But that was luck.'
'So when the auto is slow, it's traffic, and when the bus is fast, it's luck?'
Payal opened her mouth, then closed it. 'Okay, that sounds bad when you say it.'
'I'm not saying the bus is faster. I don't know either.'
'Then why are you arguing?'
'I'm not. I'm asking how you know.'
She thought. 'I don't, really. I just hate the bus because it's crowded.'
'That's a real reason. Just not a speed reason.'
'Fine. Let's time both next month.'

qa.q: How long did the auto take last week?
qa.a: It took forty minutes.

qa.q: What did Payal realise when she said 'that sounds bad when you say it'?
qa.a: She realised she had been explaining away evidence that did not fit her belief, and felt a bit embarrassed at being caught out.

qa.q: What did Amandeep's approach get right?
qa.a: He asked how she knew instead of claiming the opposite, which let her find the flaw herself.

qa.q: What would change if Amandeep had just said 'you're wrong'?
qa.a: Payal would likely have dug in and defended the auto instead of admitting she didn't really know.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager noticing that dislike of the bus, not evidence, was driving her certainty, and admitting what she does not know.
